planting.note: Set rooted plugs or cuttings into loose foredune sand in spring once nights stay reliably above the mid-50s.

directions: Beach morning glory roots at each leaf node as its trailing stems creep across open sand, forming a low mat that helps stabilize the foredune alongside sea oats and railroad vine. Establish plugs or rooted cuttings in loose, well-drained sand in full sun during spring, watering only until new growth appears since established plants draw on deep taproots for moisture. Pale pink to white funnel-shaped flowers open in the morning through the warm season and close by midday. Once rooted, the vine tolerates salt spray, burial by shifting sand, and extended drought without supplemental care.

planting.note: Broadcast seed or set plugs into lean, sandy soil in full sun after the last frost.

directions: Pinewoods fingergrass forms neat, low clumps of flattened, finger-like seed spikes held above wiry blue-green foliage, making it a useful fine-textured edging grass for sandy coastal plantings. Direct-sow or set out plugs in full sun on well-drained sandy soil in spring; it establishes quickly and self-sows modestly without becoming aggressive. It needs no fertilizer and little irrigation once rooted, thriving in the same lean, salt-influenced soils as dune and maritime forest edge plantings. Mow or shear old growth in late winter to refresh the clump before new spring growth emerges.

planting.note: Sow or plant into loose, well-drained dune sand in spring; clumps take a full season to anchor well against wind.

directions: Seaside little bluestem is the coastal dune counterpart of the familiar prairie grass, with shorter, bluer, more sprawling growth adapted to drifting sand and salt spray on barrier island foredunes. Start clumps from spring-sown seed or nursery plugs set into loose, well-drained sand in full sun, spacing plants to allow for lateral spread as the crown anchors shifting dunes. Foliage holds a blue-gray cast through summer before turning copper-orange in fall, and seed heads persist into winter for birds. Avoid rich soil or regular fertilizing, which causes floppy growth; this grass performs best on the lean, fast-draining sand it evolved with.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring after frost risk passes, siting young trees in dappled shade until established.

directions: Blolly is a slow-growing maritime hammock tree whose smooth gray bark and glossy, leathery leaves give it an almost topiary-like presence in coastal hardwood canopies from central Florida's barrier islands south through the Keys. Transplant container-grown trees in spring into well-drained, sandy or limestone-based soil, siting them where they can receive partial shade while young and fuller sun as they mature into the canopy. Small inconspicuous flowers give way to bright red, football-shaped fruit relished by songbirds and mockingbirds. Once established it tolerates salt spray, brief flooding, and drought, needing only occasional pruning to remove deadwood.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in sharply drained sandy or limestone soil, watering regularly through the first establishment season only.

directions: Darling plum is a dense, small-leaved hammock tree or large shrub valued in South Florida coastal landscapes for its tight, rounded form and tolerance of salt, wind, and poor limestone or sandy soils. Plant container stock in spring in a partly shaded to sunny site with sharp drainage, and water regularly only for the first season until the deep root system is established. Inconspicuous flowers are followed by small, sweet, dark purple-black fruit that ripens over winter and draws birds and small mammals. Its slow growth and dense branching make it a popular choice for clipped hedges and screens in maritime hammock restoration and coastal yards alike.

planting.note: Direct-sow into lean, well-drained sand in full sun in spring; plants return from a deep taproot and resent transplanting once established.

directions: Tread-softly is a low, clump-forming wildflower of coastal dunes and sandhills whose fragrant, white, star-shaped flowers open in early morning to attract sphinx moths and other long-tongued pollinators. Direct-sow seed in spring into lean, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, and site it away from paths or play areas since every part of the plant is covered in stinging hairs that cause a burning rash on contact. Established plants return each year from a deep, fleshy taproot and tolerate drought, salt spray, and infertile soil without any supplemental feeding. Handle only with gloves when thinning or removing spent growth, and let it self-sow in naturalistic pollinator plantings where its sting poses little risk.
